Delivery Driver Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)

A delivery driver resume has to prove one thing above all: that you can run a route on time, handle the parcels and the customers, and bring the vehicle back clean. Hiring managers do not hire on a list of vehicles. They hire on licence class, route range, and a record of on-time deliveries with a clean safety record.

This guide gives you a full annotated example, the skills hiring sides scan for, and the mistakes that cost interviews.

The example below is fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern that works.

Quick answer: A delivery driver resume should open with your licence class and driving record, name the routes, vehicles, and delivery volumes you handled, show on-time delivery and safety records, list your licences and certifications, and prove reliability on real routes — then keep the layout single-column with standard headings so tracking systems parse every section cleanly.

Key Takeaways

  • Lead with your licence class and driving record — what you are licensed to drive, and where.
  • Prove reliability with on-time delivery kept, failed deliveries cut, and miles driven safely.
  • Name the routes, vehicles, and scale from the posting.
  • Every bullet pairs a task with a result: what you delivered, where, and what changed.
  • Keep the file single-column with standard headings and real text, so tracking systems parse it cleanly.

What Delivery Hiring Managers Actually Look For

Talk to a dispatch manager or a fleet supervisor and you will not hear "passionate about driving." You will hear:

  • Licence class and driving record. A clean licence, the right class for the vehicle, and no at-fault accidents — checked before anything else.
  • Route range. Urban drops, suburban rounds, rural runs, multi-drop routes, and long-haul legs — name the routes and vehicles you actually drove.
  • On-time delivery kept. A route finished on schedule, a parcel delivered first time, a customer kept happy. "120 stops a day, on time" is a hiring signal; "worked hard" is not.
  • Load handling and proof of delivery. Loading, securing, scanning, and signing — and sorting the paperwork so nothing goes missing. Careful handling beats fast driving.
  • Safety and vehicle care. Daily checks, fuel and defect reports, and a clean safety record. A resume with no mention of safe driving tells a hiring manager your work is a risk.

If your resume reads like a vehicle list — all vans and trucks, no routes — it will lose to a delivery record.

Delivery Driver Resume Example

Below is a complete example for a delivery driver with parcel, food, and multi-drop route experience. It is fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern that works.

DANIEL CARTER — Delivery Driver
Columbus, OH · (614) 555-0147 · daniel.carter@email.com · Class C Licence · Clean Driving Record

SUMMARY
Delivery driver with 6 years of parcel and multi-drop route work. Ran a 120-stop urban route for a national courier, kept on-time delivery at 98% across 45,000 miles a year, and held a zero-accident record for 4 years. Vans, box trucks, and refrigerated units; Class C licence, forklift certified, DOT medical card current.

LICENCES & CERTIFICATIONS
Class C Driving Licence · DOT Medical Card · Forklift Operator Certification · Defensive Driving Course · Food Handler Certificate

SKILLS
Multi-drop route driving · Parcel sorting & scanning · Proof of delivery · Route planning & GPS navigation · Load securing & handling · Refrigerated transport · Customer service · Cash & card handling · Vehicle checks & defect reporting · Time management · Warehouse loading · Handheld scanner operation

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

Delivery Driver — SwiftParcel Couriers, Columbus, OH | 2021–Present - Ran a 120-stop urban route every day, finishing on schedule with 98% on-time delivery across 45,000 miles a year - Cut failed deliveries from 9% to 3% with a pre-route call and text routine, saving 60 redelivery hours in one year - Handled 200 parcels a day at peak season, keeping damage claims at zero with careful loading and route checks - Traced a recurring mis-sort two earlier drivers had missed, using scanner logs to find the bay error and fix it the same week - Train 3 new drivers; two of my trainees passed their route assessments on the first attempt

Delivery Driver — FreshRoute Foods, Columbus, OH | 2019–2021 - Ran 40 chilled drops a day to restaurants and cafes, keeping every load inside its temperature window - Drove refrigerated vans across 8 county routes, including early-morning bakery runs and late-night restocks - Read route sheets and marked up delivery windows, catching 5 timing clashes before they reached the road - Covered the lead driver's holidays, running the full county round end to end with no missed drops

Courier Driver — CityDrop Logistics, Columbus, OH | 2018–2019 - Worked same-day courier runs across the city, learning the pace of a real delivery schedule - Collected and delivered 60 parcels a day on a tight downtown loop, with a zero-missed-collection record in the final year - Earned promotion to route driver after completing the induction and passing the driving assessment

EDUCATION
High School Diploma — West High School, Columbus, OH, 2018 Defensive Driving Course — National Safety Council, 2021

Why it works: the summary leads with the two things delivery hiring managers check first — licence class and a delivery record kept on time (120 stops, 98% on-time, 45,000 miles) — then names the vehicles. Every bullet pairs a task with a result: fewer failed deliveries, faster routes, a crew trained.

Section-by-Section Breakdown

Summary: licence, scope, delivery record

"Class C licence," "120-stop urban route," "98% on-time delivery," "45,000 miles a year" — four facts that place you in thirty seconds. Lead with licence and a result, not training.

Experience: jobs with outcomes, not duties

"Drove a van for a courier" is a duty; "cut failed deliveries from 9% to 3% while holding the route schedule" is proof. Stops per day, parcels handled, on-time rates, and miles driven are the metrics that matter.

Routes and vehicles: proof you can drive the trade

Your range is the closest thing to proof a delivery driver gets. Name the routes you actually drove — urban multi-drop, chilled food runs, county rounds — and the vehicles behind them. One vague claim costs more than a missing skill — list only work you could do tomorrow.

Skills: mirror the posting, honestly

List the vehicles and tools you have actually worked with, in the posting's own words — "multi-drop route driving" versus "driving work" matters to filters, as does "proof of delivery" versus "deliveries." Depth in one part of the trade beats a long list.

Delivery Driver Skills & ATS Keywords

Mirror the posting's language exactly — "multi-drop route driving" vs "driving work" matters to filters:

  • Driving: multi-drop route driving, urban delivery routes, rural runs, long-haul legs, refrigerated transport, box truck driving, van driving
  • Work types: parcel delivery, food delivery, courier runs, same-day delivery, scheduled drops, warehouse loading, peak-season cover
  • Safety & handling: clean driving record, defensive driving, vehicle checks, defect reporting, load securing, DOT compliance, inspection readiness
  • Tools & reading: route planning, GPS navigation, handheld scanner, proof of delivery, load sheets, customer signatures, time management

Delivery companies screen resumes through applicant tracking systems, and multi-column layouts and text-in-graphics are the usual parsing killers. 5 Mistakes That Cost Delivery Drivers Interviews

  1. A vehicle list, not a delivery record. A long list of vehicles with no routes, stops, or deliveries reads as a hobbyist. Add numbers that show you finished it.
  2. Hiding the licence class. If your licence class and driving record are buried at the bottom, a hiring manager may never reach them. Put licence in the summary and header.
  3. Duties without results. "Delivered parcels in the city" could describe anyone on a route. Add the result — fewer failed deliveries, faster routes, a driver trained — to every bullet.
  4. Vague route claims. List what you drove, route after route.
  5. Ignoring safety and vehicle care. A resume with no mention of daily checks, defect reports, or a clean safety record tells a hiring manager your work is a risk. Put safety up front.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a commercial licence to work as a delivery driver?

It depends on the vehicle. Most parcel and food delivery vans run on a standard licence, while larger box trucks and lorries need a commercial licence class. Check the posting for the vehicle class, and list your exact licence class at the top of your resume so the hiring manager sees it first.

What experience should a new delivery driver put on a resume?

Lead with jobs and scope. A courier run on a busy city loop, a warehouse loading shift, or a food delivery round all count. Name what you delivered, how many stops, and what changed — the same pattern as a senior bullet.

How do I show on-time delivery and reliability on a delivery driver resume?

Name the record: stops per day, on-time rates kept, and miles driven — failed deliveries cut, peak-season parcels handled, routes finished on schedule. "120 stops a day with 98% on-time delivery" tells a manager more than any adjective.

Should a delivery driver resume include photos of my vehicle or work?

No — keep the resume itself text-only so tracking systems can parse it, and put vehicle or route photos in a separate portfolio or social profile linked from the header. A photo inside the resume file is usually stripped or misread by the parser.

How long should a delivery driver resume be?

One page for most delivery drivers, including experienced ones. Two pages only if you carry a long career across different work — parcel routes, food delivery, courier runs — and even then keep your best numbers on page one.

Do I need to list every job I have ever held as a delivery driver?

No. List the jobs that show your route range and your most recent work — usually the last 10 to 15 years, including your first courier or warehouse role if it is your foundation. Older short roles can be dropped, but keep the timeline honest: a gap with no explanation raises more questions than a short role ever will.
